question.prompt: The number of distinct pairs \((x,y)\) of real numbers satisfying both of the following equations: \[ \begin{aligned} x&=x^2+y^2,\\ y&=2xy. \end{aligned} \] is

solutions.explanation:
The second equation can be written as
\[
y(1-2x)=0.
\]
This makes it useful to separate the cases \(y=0\) and \(y\ne0\).

If \(y=0\), the first equation becomes \(x=x^2\), or \(x(x-1)=0\). This gives the two pairs \((0,0)\) and \((1,0)\).

If \(y\ne0\), the second equation forces \(1-2x=0\), so \(x=\tfrac12\). Substitution into the first equation gives
\[
y^2=\frac12-\frac14=\frac14.
\]
Thus \(y=\tfrac12\) or \(y=-\tfrac12\), giving \((\tfrac12,\tfrac12)\) and \((\tfrac12,-\tfrac12)\).

Every solution belongs to exactly one of these cases, and each listed pair satisfies both original equations. There are \(2+2=4\) distinct pairs, choice E.
solutions.title: Split into zero and nonzero cases

solutions.explanation:
Adding and subtracting the given equations creates perfect squares:
\[
\begin{aligned}
x+y&=(x+y)^2,\\
x-y&=(x-y)^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
These equations suggest setting \(u=x+y\) and \(v=x-y\). They give \(u(u-1)=0\) and \(v(v-1)=0\), so each of \(u\) and \(v\) must be either \(0\) or \(1\).

To check that every combination works, recover
\[
x=\frac{u+v}{2},\qquad y=\frac{u-v}{2}.
\]
Since \(u^2=u\) and \(v^2=v\), these values satisfy
\[
\begin{aligned}
x^2+y^2&=\frac{u^2+v^2}{2}=x,\\
2xy&=\frac{u^2-v^2}{2}=y.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus all \(2\cdot2=4\) choices produce solutions. Different choices cannot produce the same pair, because \(u=x+y\) and \(v=x-y\) can be recovered from that pair. There are exactly \(4\) distinct pairs, choice E.
